topics: Recent cost spike analysis (token mix + batching)

Next quarter pilot expansion and cost guardrails
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ava Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. good morning, afternoon depending on where you are. we'll try to keep to 50 minutes.
[00:00:12] Maya Chen: morning ava, thanks. we wanted to focus on that spike last week and also get clarity on timeline for private deployment.
[00:00:23] Raj Patel: yeah we had some infra questions, and lina has notes on the peering.
[00:00:30] Lina Torres: hi all, sorry if i talk over anyone. i just want to say the firewall team flagged some ephemeral ports during the stress window.
[00:00:45] Ava Morgan: perfect, yes we'll get to that. jonah, quick intro?
[00:00:50] Jonah Park: yeah hey everyone, i'm Jonah, i'm the solutions engineer on the account. i'll cover latency and the bench plan, and walk through the rollout options.
[00:00:59] Maya Chen: great, thanks jonah.
[00:01:15] Jonah Park: ok, jumping in. first pass - cost spike looks like combination of a token mix shift (more long-form docs), and our auto-batching kicking in suboptimally when sequence length variance increased. we saw the average sequence length go from ~220 to ~680 on the weekend window. that led to more KV cache misses and less effective batching.
[00:01:42] Priya Narayan: sorry did you say KV cash? do you mean KV cache?
[00:01:46] Jonah Park: yes kv cache, sorry, transcription — and that caused more memory pressure so we fell back to smaller batch sizes which increased per-token cost.
[00:01:55] Connor Blake: is that something we can tune on our side, or is it server config?
[00:02:02] Jonah Park: a little of both. we can tune prefix caching policies and advise prompt-level guardrails on your end — e.g., truncate some system tokens or normalize prompt templates — but on the platform side we can pin a quantization profile and adjust batching windows to prefer latency or throughput.
[00:02:19] Raj Patel: how does that interact with dedicated capacity? if we reserved a dedicated pool would that make batching more predictable?
[00:02:26] Jonah Park: yes dedicated generally gives much more predictable throughput and steady tail latency, because your batcher isn't sharing GPU queues with noisy neighbors. but cost is higher unless you fill commit. We discussed burst options in the contract — you can have a small dedicated base and burst to hosted for peaks to save on commit.
[00:02:47] Maya Chen: the cost numbers we saw were surprising; is there a quick rule of thumb you can give about sequence length impact?
[00:02:55] Jonah Park: rule of thumb — token cost scales roughly linearly, but long sequences increase KV cache size and may reduce batching efficiency. doubling average length can increase per-call cost by 1.8-2x depending on cache hits.
[00:03:10] Lina Torres: so the thing we should do is limit the max tokens per request? our product sends whole docs at once currently.
[00:03:16] Ava Morgan: that's a good product change. Connor, can you speak to why you're sending whole docs now?
[00:03:22] Connor Blake: we wanted fewer round trips, simpler UX — but maybe we need to chunk and reassemble client-side.
[00:03:29] Maya Chen: we can change that, but need a rollout plan because it's in prod.
[00:03:33] Jonah Park: for rollout we recommend a staged chunking approach, start with non-critical flows and measure latency/cost delta. also we can enable prefix caching on the server to reduce repeated attention on identical preambles.
[00:03:46] [00:04:02] Ava Morgan: switching to latency. Jonah, you had a couple of graphs?
[00:04:10] Jonah Park: yes, on the bench we saw tail latency (95/99th) spike for sequences >1024 tokens. there were a few outliers caused by cold KV cache as the model tried to load additional kv shards. our mitigation: eager KV prefetch for pinned contexts, smaller attention chunking, and model variant with a faster attention kernel for long sequences.
[00:04:35] Priya Narayan: is that a model change or a runtime flag?
[00:04:38] Jonah Park: runtime flag mostly, but the model variant requires switching to a variant compiled with attention optimizations — it's compatible but you'll want to test quality.
[00:04:48] Raj Patel: you mentioned quality regressions earlier. how safe is the fallback?
[00:04:52] Jonah Park: we have canary + A/B guardrails. Redwood Optimize can run diff evals versus your eval set, and trigger rollback if generation divergence is above threshold. We'll run evals as part of the pilot.
[00:05:04] Maya Chen: good.
[00:05:12] Lina Torres: quick security question — our security team asked for KMS integration and audit log retention. where are we on that?
[00:05:20] Sofia Delgado: we've got KMS integrations across hosted and dedicated. for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and more strict audit retention. i can share the security pack after this call.
[00:05:32] Raj Patel: do you have SOC 2 cert?
[00:05:34] Sofia Delgado: yes SOC 2 Type II — we'll attach the report and the network diagram.
[00:05:40] Connor Blake: thanks. that will help the security review board.
[00:05:50] Maya Chen: timeline question — if we commit to a small dedicated pool and plan private later, how long until private deployment (VPC)?
[00:05:58] Ava Morgan: typical private timeline is 6-8 weeks from signed SOW depending on onboarding windows and infra approval. dedicated is faster — we can reserve capacity in 2-3 weeks with the right commit.
[00:06:12] Raj Patel: what about data residency? we need EU region for some workloads.
[00:06:17] Ava Morgan: we support region pinning for workloads; Private gives you the most control. Hosted also supports region selection for model endpoints for EU.
[00:06:26] Maya Chen: can you also explain the pilot expansion we talked about?
[00:06:30] Ava Morgan: yes the pilot expansion would add an additional route for your higher throughput flow, and we'll allocate canary capacity and run the model v2.1 on 10% traffic with fallback to current v2.0. That lets you measure quality and cost delta.
[00:06:45] Priya Narayan: what are the expected cost deltas for v2.1?
[00:06:49] Jonah Park: early estimates show v2.1 is slightly more compute-heavy per token but includes better caching behavior which can offset the increase. net delta depends on prompt mix — we'll run your prompts through the evaluation harness and return a delta sheet.
[00:07:03] [00:07:40] Maya Chen: ok let's talk about instrumentation — we need token-level breakdowns and error traces in console.
[00:07:47] Sofia Delgado: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, traces for 500s and 429s. we can add a dashboard for your product routes and link to your Sentry/Datadog via webhooks.
[00:08:06] Lina Torres: can we get a per-user cost signal for chargeback?
[00:08:10] Ava Morgan: yes, token-level attribution is possible with route-level tagging; we'll work with your billing team to map routes -> internal cost centers.
[00:08:20] Connor Blake: great.
[00:08:30] Jonah Park: quick note on benchmarks: to reproduce spike we'll need a representative 7-day sample, and we'll run a mix of static evals and live replay in a staging cluster. replay timing should mimic your concurrency distribution.
[00:08:44] Maya Chen: we'll send that.
[00:08:50] Raj Patel: any gotchas for the VPC peering? Lina, can you say what you saw?
[00:08:56] Lina Torres: sure — peering requires specific ASN ranges and not to overlap with our existing VPC CIDRs. also we need to allow certain ephemeral port ranges for the GPU control plane. i'll share a checklist.
[00:09:10] Ava Morgan: perfect. i'll flag that and Sofia will attach the network diagram.
[00:09:22] [00:10:00] (15 min went by — mid-call notes omitted)
[00:25:12] Jonah Park: returning to cost guardrails — we suggest two levers: prompt-side normalization (truncate/shorten system tokens), and server-side pinning of batch windows at the route level. combine those with a cost alert on per-route $/hour.
[00:25:30] Priya Narayan: can you set an alert threshold for the next spike?
[00:25:34] Sofia Delgado: we can create a cost monitor and threshold; if a route exceeds baseline by 30% we'll push an alert to slack + PagerDuty.
[00:25:44] Maya Chen: that will help.
[00:25:50] Raj Patel: what about model fallback logic? we want to degrade gracefully to a cheaper model during sustained peaks.
[00:25:58] Jonah Park: you can set automatic fallback policies: if latency or cost crosses threshold we route to a compatible smaller model and flag an incident. Redwood Console supports policy config and pre-warmed fallbacks.
[00:26:10] Connor Blake: are there sample configs we can copy?
[00:26:13] Jonah Park: yes i'll send a sample policy repo and a runbook.
[00:26:20] [00:30:00] (brief cross-talk)
[00:31:02] Maya Chen: on the security docs — any special compliance for healthcare workloads?
[00:31:08] Sofia Delgado: we have a HIPAA compliance kit for Private deployments, plus BAAs available. Hosted can be used under certain constraints but Private is recommended for PHI.
[00:31:20] Raj Patel: noted.
[00:31:28] Ava Morgan: ok let's recap actions — we'll share the pricing sheet, security pack, and sample fallback configs. Jonah will run the bench once we get the sample traffic. Arborlytics will send sample data and confirm peering constraints.
[00:31:46] Maya Chen: timeline sounds good.
[00:32:00] Priya Narayan: question — any blockers on your side for a 2-3 week dedicated reservation?
[00:32:06] Ava Morgan: sign-off and a PO are the typical gating items. if procurement is ready we can spin up reserved capacity in ~14 business days.
[00:32:18] Raj Patel: procurement will need the SOW; can you send that with the pricing?
[00:32:22] Ava Morgan: yes will do.
[00:32:30] Lina Torres: and i'll follow up on the firewall rules and share the checklist.
[00:32:35] Jonah Park: one more thing — we saw in the replay a handful of 429s tied to sudden concurrency bursts; adding a leaky-bucket on the client gateway reduces those without dropping requests.
[00:32:47] Connor Blake: we can add client-side smoothing.
[00:32:53] Maya Chen: ok thanks.
[00:40:00] (final 10 minutes — scheduling + wrap)
[00:40:12] Ava Morgan: next step dates — i'll get pricing and security docs out by thursday, Jonah will do the bench after Maya's sample, and we'll meet again for the latency deep-dive on 2026-02-18. does that work for everyone?
[00:40:30] Maya Chen: yes that works.
[00:40:35] Raj Patel: yes.
[00:41:00] Ava Morgan: awesome. thanks everyone for the candid details. we'll follow up in email with links: deck: https://redwood.example.com/arborlytics-qbr-deck and bench-run template: https://redwood.example.com/bench-templates.
[00:41:20] Priya Narayan: appreciate it.
[00:41:30] Sofia Delgado: i'll upload SOC2 + network diagram to the secure link.
[00:41:45] Maya Chen: great, talk soon.
[00:41:52] (meeting ends)
